walkthroughs.body_html:
Space Physics — a core area of GCSE Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Space Physics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Space Physics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Redshift of distant galaxies is evidence that:
options: the universe is contracting
galaxies are heating up
the universe is expanding
light slows over distance

mcqs.q: The Sun is currently in which stage?
options: Protostar
Main sequence
Red giant
White dwarf

mcqs.q: If air resistance is ignored, which falls faster: a heavy ball or a light ball dropped from the same height?
options: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter objects because gravity pulls more on them.
No — it is caused by dust in space absorbing blue light.
The lighter ball falls faster because it has less inertia.
Both fall at the same rate because gravitational acceleration is independent of mass.

mcqs.q: Is the cosmological redshift of distant galaxies a true Doppler shift?
options: No — it is caused by dust in space absorbing blue light.
Yes — it is the same Doppler shift as a moving siren on Earth.
The force is in the same direction as the current in the wire.
No — it arises from the expansion of space stretching photon wavelengths during transit, not from the galaxy's motion through space.

mcqs.q: In what direction does a magnetic field exert a force on a current-carrying wire?
options: Perpendicular to both the current direction and the magnetic field direction (Fleming's left hand rule).
The lighter ball falls faster because it has less inertia.
The force is in the same direction as the magnetic field.
The force is in the same direction as the current in the wire.
